topic: the concept of work done against gravity (lifting objects)

easy.text: What is the formula for work done when lifting an object straight up against gravity?

options.feedback: Correct -- since the force needed equals the object's weight, work equals weight times the vertical distance lifted.
Work is calculated by multiplying, not adding, weight and height.
This isn't the correct relationship -- work involves multiplying, not dividing.

options.text: Work = height only, regardless of weight
options.feedback: Work also depends directly on the object's weight, not height alone.

medium.text: How much work is done lifting a 50 N object to a height of 3 meters?

options.feedback: Correct -- work = weight × height = 50×3=150.
This adds the values instead of multiplying them.
This divides instead of multiplying weight by height.
This ignores the height factor entirely.

hard.text: Two people lift identical 20 kg boxes to the same height of 2 meters, but Person A does it in 5 seconds while Person B takes 10 seconds. How do the amounts of WORK done by each person compare?

options.text: The work done is exactly the same for both, since work depends only on force and distance, not time
options.feedback: Correct -- while their POWER output differs (Person A is more powerful, doing the same work in less time), the actual work done is identical since force and distance are the same.

options.text: Person A did twice as much work as Person B
options.feedback: Work depends on force and distance, not time -- since both lifted the same weight the same height, they did the same amount of work, though Person A had more power.

options.text: Person B did twice as much work as Person A
options.feedback: This is backwards, and also incorrect regardless -- work depends on force and distance only, and both did the same amount of work despite the time difference.

options.text: Work cannot be calculated without knowing the exact time taken
options.feedback: Work specifically does NOT depend on time -- it can be calculated purely from force and distance, which are identical in both cases.

easy.hard: This calculation combines how much an object weighs with how far up it's raised.
easy.medium: Multiply the object's weight by how high it's lifted.
easy.easy: Multiply weight by height to get work.

medium.hard: Multiply the weight value by the height value.

hard.hard: Work is defined purely in terms of force and displacement, independent of the time taken -- time only affects the related but distinct quantity of power.
hard.medium: Since work only cares about force and distance, not how fast it happened, both people technically did the same amount of work.
hard.easy: Since work only cares about the weight and the height, not the time it took, both people did the same amount of work.

topic: the concept of a system's total mechanical energy (KE + PE)

easy.text: What is total mechanical energy generally the sum of?

options.feedback: Correct -- mechanical energy combines the energy of motion (kinetic) and the energy of position (potential).
These are different forms of energy, not what typically makes up mechanical energy.
Mass and volume are physical properties, not forms of energy.

options.text: Only kinetic energy, with nothing else
options.feedback: Mechanical energy includes both kinetic AND potential energy, not kinetic energy alone.

medium.text: As a ball falls from a height (ignoring air resistance), what happens to its TOTAL mechanical energy?

options.text: It stays constant, since energy just converts from potential to kinetic form
options.feedback: Correct -- without energy loss to air resistance, total mechanical energy is conserved even as its form shifts.

options.text: It continuously increases as the ball falls
options.feedback: Without an outside energy input, total mechanical energy shouldn't increase -- it stays constant, just changing form.

options.text: It continuously decreases as the ball falls
options.feedback: Without energy loss (like air resistance), total mechanical energy doesn't decrease -- it remains constant.

options.text: It becomes exactly zero the instant the ball starts falling
options.feedback: Total mechanical energy doesn't drop to zero -- it's conserved throughout the fall, just shifting between potential and kinetic forms.

hard.text: A roller coaster car at the top of a hill has 500 J of potential energy and 0 J of kinetic energy. Ignoring friction, what is its kinetic energy at the bottom of the hill, where potential energy is 0 J?

options.feedback: Correct -- since total mechanical energy (500 J) is conserved, all of it converts to kinetic energy when potential energy reaches 0.
This would mean all the energy simply vanished, which contradicts the conservation of mechanical energy.
This doubles the energy without justification -- total mechanical energy should remain constant at 500 J, not increase.
This assumes only half the energy converted, but with no friction, ALL of the potential energy should convert to kinetic energy.

easy.hard: This total combines the energy of motion with the energy stored due to position.
easy.medium: This total combines the energy of movement with the energy of position/height.
easy.easy: This is kinetic energy plus potential energy added together.

medium.hard: Without energy loss to outside forces, the sum of kinetic and potential energy remains constant throughout the motion.
medium.medium: As height-based energy decreases, motion-based energy increases by the same amount, keeping the total the same.
medium.easy: As the ball loses height energy, it gains the same amount of motion energy -- the total stays the same.

hard.hard: Since total mechanical energy is conserved, whatever potential energy is lost must be exactly converted into an equal amount of kinetic energy.
hard.medium: Since total energy stays the same, whatever potential energy is lost, kinetic energy gains the same amount.
hard.easy: Since total energy stays the same, whatever potential energy is lost, kinetic energy gains that exact amount.
